title: Sask. RCMP don't support inquest recommendation for medic in cell areas
subtitle: The RCMP's formal response said "it is not within the ability of the RCMP to train members to this level of health care."
article: Roseanne McCallum says the jury's recommendations at the end of the inquest into her son's 2018 death in RCMP custody were good and could prevent another death - if they were followed.
She was upset by the Saskatchewan RCMP's response, she said.

The jury that sat for the July inquest into the death of Trevor McCallum made 14 recommendations , including 11 to the RCMP, two to the provincial government and one to the Corps of Commissionaires, which is contracted by the RCMP to provide guards for holding cell areas.

McCallum died on April 10, 2018 after he was found unresponsive in the cell area of the Meadow Lake RCMP detachment. Jurors found he died of an accidental overdose of methamphetamine and an antidepressant .

The inquest heard that throughout the night of April 9, he was pacing in a cell, singing, dancing, climbing on concrete benches and removing his clothes, and that guards brought concerns to RCMP members who checked on him but concluded he wasn't having a medical emergency .

Rhonda Blackmore, assistant commissioner and commanding officer for the RCMP's "F" Division (Saskatchewan), provided the RCMP's Sept. 27 response to the jury's recommendations in a letter to Chief Coroner Clive Weighill.

The response said the RCMP did not support a recommendation that a medic be present in holding facilities with eight or more inmates, or to have a medic assess everyone in small facilities every four hours. Blackmore's response said "it is not within the ability of the RCMP to train members to this level of health care."

The RCMP also disagreed with a recommendation to require medical assessments for people behaving in a manner consistent with drug intoxication for four hours, saying its policy is already to require continual assessment for responsiveness and to require a medical assessment for someone showing signs of "injury or illness for which medical attention should be sought."
Since Trevor's death, RCMP now require a medical assessment if someone is brought into detention sober and later begins to show signs of impairment.
Roseanne said she wanted the four-hour requirement implemented because medical assessment would be necessary if a person has not come down from a drug or gets worse after four hours.
"My son, I think, would gave been alive today if they had got him the medical assessment that night," she wrote in a Facebook message on Tuesday.

The jury also recommended the Meadow Lake detachment adopt 24-hour policing. RCMP said the municipal government and the province have discussed additional funding and officers, but there's no certainty about whether it will happen.

The jury recommended RCMP train staff to recognize symptoms of "specific drug intoxication" and overdose in all relevant drugs. RCMP said the training is already integrated in other areas, such as impaired driver and standardized field sobriety training, drug recognition expert training and "on the job experience."
The RCMP agreed in principle to a recommendation that it look into a technological solution to monitor vital signs of people in custody.

In the Commissionaires's Sept, 20 response letter , Lorne Gelowitz, CEO for the North Saskatchewan division, said guards will now be told they can request medical assessments and they will receive training on recognizing signs of drug intoxication and overdose.

Saskatchewan RCMP declined further comment. T he provincial Ministry of Health said in an email it is reviewing the recommendations and a response will be provided to the coroner's service upon completion.
